articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than construction. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 3 of 47 planned drainage projects
Public records show $8.1 million went to engineering consultants while construction contracts totaled $4.3 million
County staff cite permitting delays and a 2024 reorganization that left the stormwater division without a director for 11 months
articles.body:
The intersection of Fairfield Drive and Davis Highway floods every time it rains more than two inches. Water pools in the low spot where the roads meet, swallows the right lane, and backs up traffic for a quarter mile in each direction. The county has known about this since at least 2019.

It remains on a list of 47 priority stormwater projects. It has not been fixed.

Three years after Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee—marketed as the solution to chronic flooding that costs residents thousands in property damage annually—the county has completed exactly three projects. Public records obtained by The Flightline show where the money has actually gone: $8.1 million to engineering and consulting firms, $4.3 million to construction contractors, and the rest sitting in reserve accounts or absorbed into administrative overhead.

The fee generates roughly $15.7 million per year. At the current pace of construction, the original 47-project list would take more than four decades to complete.

The Promise

In November 2022, county commissioners asked voters to approve a stormwater utility fee. The pitch was straightforward: a monthly charge on property owners—averaging $7.50 for residential parcels—would fund drainage improvements the general budget couldn't cover.

Campaign materials produced by the county listed specific projects. Culvert replacements in Bellview. Retention pond expansions near the airport. Channel improvements along Eleven Mile Creek. The documents promised "measurable progress within the first two years."

Voters approved the measure 58% to 42%.

"People were tired of flooding," said Sandra Mitchell, who lives in the Brownsville area and supported the fee. "We were told this would fix it. That was the whole point."

The Reality

The Flightline filed public records requests for all stormwater fee expenditures, contracts, and project status reports from January 2023 through May 2026. The documents tell a different story than the one commissioners presented to voters.

Of the $47.2 million collected:

  • $8.1 million went to three engineering firms for design work, feasibility studies, and project management
  • $4.3 million funded actual construction on three completed projects
  • $6.8 million covers salaries and benefits for stormwater division staff
  • $3.2 million paid for equipment purchases and maintenance
  • $24.8 million remains in designated reserve accounts

The three completed projects: a culvert replacement on Klondike Road, a drainage ditch improvement near Scenic Heights, and a small retention pond expansion in Ferry Pass. Combined construction cost: $4.3 million. Combined population served: approximately 2,400 households.

The Fairfield Drive flooding remains. So does the chronic drainage failure in Brownsville. So do the 44 other projects on the priority list.

What Went Wrong

County officials point to several factors. None fully explain the gap between revenue and results.

Permitting delays with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection slowed two major projects involving wetland-adjacent work. State records confirm permits for the Eleven Mile Creek channel project took 14 months to process—seven months longer than typical.

But permitting doesn't explain why the county spent nearly twice as much on consultants as construction. It doesn't explain the $24.8 million sitting in reserves while residents continue flooding.

The larger issue appears organizational.

In March 2024, County Administrator Wes Moreno reorganized the Public Works department. The stormwater division was merged with road maintenance under a single director. The previous stormwater director, Carlos Vega, left for a position in Hillsborough County. His replacement wasn't hired until February 2025—an 11-month gap.

During that period, according to internal emails obtained through records requests, project timelines slipped. Contractors complained about delayed responses. One email from a project manager at Baskerville-Donovan Engineers noted: "We have completed designs for four priority projects but have no county point of contact to approve moving to bid phase."

The email is dated September 2024. Two of those four projects still haven't gone to bid.

The Consultant Question

The $8.1 million in consulting and engineering fees raises its own questions.

Three firms received the bulk of the work: Baskerville-Donovan Engineers ($3.4 million), AECOM ($2.8 million), and Dewberry Engineers ($1.9 million). All three have done business with Escambia County for years. All three have contributed to county commissioner campaigns, though state law permits such contributions and no evidence suggests improper influence.

What the contracts show is a reliance on outside expertise for work that a fully staffed county department might handle internally. Design work. Feasibility studies. Project management. Bid document preparation.

"That's not unusual for a county this size," said Robert Chen, a public administration professor at the University of West Florida who reviewed the contracts at The Flightline's request. "What is unusual is the ratio. You'd expect to see three or four dollars in construction for every dollar in design. Here it's the opposite."

Chen said the pattern suggests either extremely complex projects—which the scope documents don't support—or a department that lacks capacity to move work from design to construction.

"You can plan forever," he said. "At some point you have to build."

The Reserves

County budget director Maria Santos defended the $24.8 million in reserves during a May budget workshop.

"Stormwater projects are multi-year endeavors," she told commissioners. "You don't spend the money the year you collect it. You accumulate funds for major capital projects."

This is true as far as it goes. Large infrastructure projects require upfront reserves to cover contracts that may span multiple budget cycles.

But the original fee proposal didn't anticipate $24.8 million sitting idle after three years. The project timeline presented to voters assumed construction would begin on at least 15 projects by now. It has begun on six. Three are complete. Three are ongoing.

The remaining 41 projects exist only on paper—some with completed designs, some with feasibility studies, some with nothing but a line item and a location.

What Residents See

Sandra Mitchell's street in Brownsville floods three or four times a year. Her garage has taken water twice since 2023. She's filed insurance claims totaling $11,000.

"I voted for this fee," she said. "I pay it every month. And my street is on the list. Has been on the list. Nothing happens."

Brownsville drainage improvements appear as Project 23 on the county's priority matrix. Current status: "Design phase—90% complete." That status hasn't changed in 18 months.

At the Fairfield and Davis intersection, business owners have adapted. Marcus Coleman, who runs an auto parts store on the corner, moved his inventory storage to higher shelving after a 2024 storm pushed water into his building.

"They told us they were going to fix this when they passed that fee," Coleman said. "Three years later, same story. Water in the street. Water in my shop if it rains hard enough."

The Fairfield Drive project is number seven on the priority list. Status: "Feasibility study complete. Design not yet funded."

What Happens Next

County commissioners will review stormwater program performance at their July 15 meeting. Staff have prepared a presentation recommending "accelerated project delivery" through expanded contractor pre-qualification and streamlined internal approval processes.

The presentation does not recommend additional construction funding. It does recommend extending the current consulting contracts.

Commissioner Doug Underhill, who voted against the original fee in 2022, said he plans to request a full audit of stormwater expenditures.

"Voters were sold a bill of goods," Underhill said. "They were told their money would fix flooding. Instead it's paying for studies and sitting in bank accounts. That's not what people voted for."

Commissioner Lumon May, who supported the fee, said the program needs time.

"Infrastructure takes years," May said. "You can't snap your fingers and fix 50 years of drainage problems. We're making progress. It's slower than any of us want, but it's progress."

The numbers suggest otherwise. At $4.3 million in construction over three years, the county is building at a pace of roughly $1.4 million annually. The 47-project list carries an estimated total cost of $89 million. At current rates, completion would come sometime around 2089.

The fee has no sunset provision. Escambia County residents will continue paying it indefinitely.

And on Fairfield Drive, when it rains more than two inches, the intersection will continue to flood.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Fishing Families of Perdido Key
articles.dek: New condo towers keep rising. The mullet runners who worked these waters for generations are down to a handful of boats.
brief: Only three mullet fishing families remain active on Perdido Key, down from more than twenty in the 1980s
Rising property values and condo development have eliminated traditional fish camps and beach access points
The Gonzalez family, fishing the same waters since 1952, may be the last to hold on
articles.body:
The nets hit the water at 4:47 a.m., before the first tower crane on Perdido Key starts moving. Ray Gonzalez stands thigh-deep in the Gulf, feeding out 600 yards of monofilament in a wide arc while his son Carlos idles the skiff along the sandbar. They've done this together for 31 years. Their grandfather did it before them.

"See that?" Ray points east, where the skeleton of a 22-story condominium rises against the pink sky. "That's where we used to pull the boats up. Had a little camp there. Concrete pilings now."

The Gonzalez family is one of three still running mullet on Perdido Key. In 1986, according to Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission records, 23 commercial fishing operations held permits for this stretch of coastline. The names read like a phone book of old Pensacola: Bonifay, Jernigan, Caro, Penton. Most sold out. Some died off. A few moved to Louisiana or the Panhandle's eastern reaches where the condos haven't come yet.

What remains is a profession measured in single digits and early mornings.

The economics of holding on

Tommy Hendrix parks his truck at a public access point three miles from where his family's fish camp stood until 2019. A developer paid his father $2.3 million for the half-acre lot. The condo that replaced it lists units starting at $1.4 million.

"Dad took the money. I don't blame him," Hendrix said. "But now I drive 40 minutes round trip just to put my boat in. Used to walk out my back door."

Hendrix, 58, figures he nets around $34,000 in a good year selling mullet to Pensacola fish houses and roe to Asian exporters during the fall spawn. His fuel costs have tripled since 2019. Ice is up 60 percent. The math doesn't work unless you own your equipment outright and don't expect health insurance.

"I'm not getting rich," he said. "I'm getting by. There's a difference."

The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office shows waterfront land on Perdido Key averaging $4.2 million per acre in 2025 assessments, up from $890,000 in 2015. For fishing families who held onto property, the tax burden alone can force a sale. For those who rent boat slips, the rates have followed the real estate.

Big Lagoon Marina, one of the last commercial-friendly operations on the key, charges $485 monthly for a 24-foot slip. In 2018, the same slip ran $180.

What the nets remember

Mullet run in schools along the beach, feeding on algae and detritus in the shallows. The fish aren't glamorous. They don't fight like redfish or photograph like tarpon. But smoked mullet built the seafood culture of the Gulf Coast, and the roe—salted, pressed, dried—commands prices in Japan and Taiwan that would surprise anyone who's watched the baitfish jump at sunset.

Ray Gonzalez learned the water from his father, Miguel, who immigrated from Cuba in 1952 and found work on the docks before saving enough to buy his own nets. The family still uses a technique Miguel brought from Havana: a specific way of mending torn mesh that Ray says he's never seen anywhere else.

"My hands know it," Ray said, holding up palms crosshatched with old scars. "Couldn't teach it if I tried. You just do it until it's part of you."

Carlos Gonzalez, 44, is the last of his generation in the family to fish. His two brothers work in Pensacola—one in HVAC, one for the county road department. His own son, 19, started at Pensacola State College in the fall studying marine biology.

"He wants to save the ocean," Carlos said without irony. "Maybe that's the better path."

A shoreline transformed

The Perdido Key of fishing camps and bait shacks exists now mostly in photographs. The Escambia County Historical Society maintains an archive of images from the 1960s and 1970s showing a coastline of small wooden structures, skiffs pulled up on sand, nets drying on racks made from driftwood.

Drive the key today and the view is different. The 16-mile barrier island holds an estimated 4,800 condo units, according to a 2024 survey by the West Florida Regional Planning Council. Another 1,200 are permitted or under construction. The new Perdido Towers development, the one visible from Ray Gonzalez's morning fishing spot, will add 340 more when it opens in 2028.

Escambia County planning documents show no commercial fishing operations listed as existing land uses on the key. The zoning maps are shaded in residential yellows and commercial reds. The fish camps that once dotted the shoreline weren't zoned at all—they predated the system, grandfathered in until the owners sold or died.

"Nobody's breaking any laws," said Marcus Webb, a Pensacola attorney who specializes in land use. "The county's comprehensive plan encourages density on barrier islands. The fishing families weren't pushed out by anything illegal. They were priced out by what the market wanted."

Morning catch

By 7:15 a.m., the Gonzalez nets are back in the boat. The haul is modest: maybe 200 pounds of mullet, plus some whiting and a few blue crabs tangled in the mesh. Ray estimates the morning's work at $180 wholesale if the fish house is buying.

Carlos steers the skiff toward the public ramp at Big Lagoon State Park, the only launch point on this stretch that doesn't charge commercial rates. The line of recreational boats waiting to put in has already formed. Families with coolers and fishing rods. Kayakers heading for the seagrass flats. A woman in a bikini taking photos of the sunrise for her phone.

The Gonzalez skiff, weathered and work-stained, looks out of place among the gleaming center consoles.

"People ask what we're doing sometimes," Carlos said. "Like they've never seen a fishing boat before."

Ray Gonzalez is 67. His knees ache from decades of standing in salt water. His doctor wants him to quit, or at least slow down. He figures he has maybe five more years of mornings like this one, if his body holds.

After that, he doesn't know. His son might keep at it. Or he might not. The nets will go somewhere—maybe a museum, maybe a dumpster. The water will remain, lapping at the shore beneath towers that keep climbing higher.

"Somebody will remember," Ray said, hauling the cooler of fish onto the dock. "Maybe not for long. But somebody."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's Expanded Flight Training Brings More Jets—and More Noise Complaints
articles.dek: The Navy added 40 aircraft to its training fleet this spring. Residents from East Hill to Gulf Breeze say they weren't warned.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola added 40 T-6B Texan II turboprops to its training fleet in March, increasing daily flight operations by roughly 35%.
Noise complaints filed with Escambia County have tripled since April, with East Hill, East Pensacola Heights, and Gulf Breeze residents reporting disruptions from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
Navy officials say they followed notification protocols, but multiple community leaders say they received no advance warning of the expansion.
articles.body:
The turboprop came in low over Bayou Texar at 6:47 a.m. on a Tuesday. Margaret Odom was standing in her backyard on 12th Avenue, coffee in hand, when the roar hit. She dropped the mug. It shattered on the patio.

"I've lived in East Hill for 31 years," Odom said. "I'm used to the Blue Angels. I'm used to some noise. This is different. This is constant."

Since March, Naval Air Station Pensacola has been operating 40 additional T-6B Texan II aircraft as part of an expanded pilot training program. The single-engine turboprops, used to train Navy and Marine Corps aviators, now fill the skies over greater Pensacola from early morning until well after dinner. Flight operations that once peaked at around 180 daily sorties have climbed to nearly 250 on busy days, according to base officials.

Residents across the region say nobody told them it was coming.

The Expansion

The additional aircraft arrived at NAS Pensacola between March 3 and March 18, part of a broader Navy initiative to address a pilot training backlog that accumulated during the pandemic years. The program, known internally as "Undergraduate Military Flight Training Acceleration," aims to push more student aviators through primary training at Pensacola, Corpus Christi, and Whiting Field.

Commander Jessica Rawlings, public affairs officer for Naval Air Training Command, confirmed the expansion in an email to The Flightline.

"Training the next generation of Naval Aviators is critical to national defense," Rawlings wrote. "NAS Pensacola has the infrastructure and airspace to support this increased capacity, and we appreciate the continued support of our neighbors in the Pensacola community."

Rawlings said the base followed standard Department of Defense protocols for community notification, including updates to the NAS Pensacola website and coordination with the Pensacola Chamber of Commerce.

But Pensacola City Council member Allison Patton, whose District 6 includes East Hill and East Pensacola Heights, said she learned about the expansion from constituents—not the Navy.

"The first I heard of it was when my phone started ringing off the hook in April," Patton said. "People wanted to know what was happening. I had no answers for them because I didn't know either."

Counting Complaints

Escambia County's noise complaint hotline logged 47 calls related to aircraft between January and March of this year. From April through June 10, that number jumped to 156.

In Gulf Breeze, the city clerk's office has received 23 written complaints since April, up from two in all of 2025. Santa Rosa County officials declined to provide specific numbers but confirmed an "uptick" in calls.

The complaints describe a pattern: flights beginning around 6 a.m., continuing through the day with brief lulls, then resuming in the early evening. Multiple residents reported aircraft noise after 9 p.m., though Navy officials say scheduled training operations end by 10 p.m. on weekdays and 6 p.m. on weekends.

Don Becher, a retired accountant who lives in the Scenic Heights neighborhood, started keeping a log in mid-April. By June 1, he had documented 847 individual aircraft passes over or near his home during daylight hours.

"I counted everything I could see or hear from my front porch," Becher said. "Some days it was 60, 70 planes. The worst day was 94."

Becher said the noise makes it impossible to hold a conversation outdoors during peak hours. His wife, who works from home as a medical transcriptionist, has started driving to the library to take calls.

Flight Patterns and Frustrations

The T-6B Texan II is louder than its predecessor, the T-34C Turbo Mentor, which the Navy retired from primary training in 2024. The T-6B's Pratt & Whitney turboprop engine produces roughly 1,100 horsepower and a distinctive high-pitched whine that carries for miles.

Training flights follow established patterns radiating out from NAS Pensacola, with aircraft climbing to altitude over Escambia Bay before heading to practice areas over the Gulf of Mexico or rural Santa Rosa County. But residents in the flight paths say the frequency has made the noise inescapable.

"It's not that any single plane is unbearable," said Tom Fitzgerald, president of the East Hill Neighborhood Association. "It's that there's another one every three minutes for 12 hours straight."

Fitzgerald said his organization requested a meeting with base officials in late April. They received a response in mid-May offering a briefing in July.

"July," Fitzgerald repeated. "The problem started in March. We asked in April. And maybe we can talk about it in July."

What the Navy Says

In a phone interview, Lieutenant Commander David Park, a spokesman for NAS Pensacola, acknowledged that flight operations have increased but pushed back on the characterization that residents were left in the dark.

"We understand that increased operations can be noticeable to our neighbors," Park said. "We make every effort to be good partners in this community. Information about our training mission is available on our website and through our community liaison office."

Park said the base conducted noise studies before the expansion and determined that the additional flights would remain within acceptable thresholds established by the Federal Aviation Administration. He declined to share the studies, citing operational security, but said residents could file Freedom of Information Act requests.

When asked why elected officials like Patton were not directly notified, Park said the base relies on established channels.

"We work with the chamber and other regional partners to disseminate information," he said. "We can't individually contact every stakeholder, but we do our best to keep the community informed."

Bethany Wainwright, vice president of communications for the Pensacola Chamber of Commerce, confirmed that the chamber received a briefing from Navy officials in February about the planned expansion.

"We were told it was coming and that it would mean more activity at the base," Wainwright said. "We shared that information with our members through our newsletter."

The chamber's newsletter reaches approximately 1,200 member businesses. It does not go to the general public.

Living With It

For now, residents have few options. NAS Pensacola operates under federal authority, exempt from local noise ordinances. The FAA oversees civilian airspace but has no jurisdiction over military training operations. Escambia County's noise hotline exists primarily to document complaints, not resolve them.

Patton said she has requested a formal briefing from Navy officials for the city council, tentatively scheduled for August. She has also asked city staff to research what, if any, legal avenues exist for the city to address the issue.

"I'm not anti-military. This is a Navy town, and we're proud of that," Patton said. "But there has to be some communication, some partnership. You can't just triple the noise and expect people to accept it because it's for national defense."

Odom, the East Hill resident who dropped her coffee mug, said she doesn't expect anything to change. She grew up in Pensacola. Her father worked at the base for 22 years. She knows how it goes.

"They'll do what they're going to do," she said. "I just wish someone had warned us. A letter. An email. Something. Instead we woke up one day and the sky was full of planes, and nobody could tell us why."

She's ordered a new set of mugs. Plastic this time.
